title: Why bond yields and term premia are likely to remain high
gist: Oxford Economics finds more than half of the rise in advanced-economy bond yields since 2020 came from the term premium, now back at mid-2000s levels, driven by bond-stock correlations that turned positive in Q3 2023. It expects both to stay high amid more frequent supply shocks and more hawkish central banks.

insights.claim: A 10-year government bond yield can be split into the expected path of safe short-term rates plus a broadly defined term premium that compensates investors for the risks of holding the bond.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Use the rates-path vs term-premium split to judge whether a yield move reflects policy expectations or a risk-compensation repricing.

insights.claim: Since 2020, more than half of the rise in advanced-economy government bond yields has come from the term premium rather than from expected short-term rates.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The yield surge is mostly a risk-compensation story, so rate-cut expectations alone will not bring yields back down.
insights.quote: Since 2020, more than half of the increase in advanced-economy government bond yields came from the term premium.

insights.claim: Term premia are back at mid-2000s levels: high relative to the last 10 years but still low in a broader historical context.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Implies there is room for term premia to rise further before reaching long-run historical norms.
insights.quote: Term premia are now back to their mid-2000s levels

themes.theme: Bond-stock correlation as term premium driver

insights.claim: Across major advanced economies, bond-stock correlations were negative for most of this century, turned positive again in Q3 2023, and have risen steeply since.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The regime in which bonds reliably offset equity drawdowns has ended, which breaks the assumptions behind classic 60/40 portfolios.

insights.claim: The strength of bond-stock co-movement is an important driver of the term premium: when bonds are a worse hedge against stock returns, investors demand more compensation to hold them.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Track the bond-stock correlation as a leading input for term-premium and long-duration pricing.
insights.locator: We find that an important driver

insights.claim: A positive bond-stock correlation resembles the 1980s and 1990s, and this time the higher term premium is required also on inflation-indexed bonds.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Inflation-linked bonds are no longer a clean refuge from the higher-premium regime.
insights.locator: This means bonds are a worse hedge

themes.theme: Regime shift: supply shocks and hawkish central banks

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects the bond-stock correlation and bond term premia to stay high because advanced economies have entered an era of more frequent supply shocks and more hawkish central banks.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Position for structurally higher long-end yields rather than a reversion to the post-2010 low-premium regime.
insights.quote: We think the bond-stock correlation and bond term premia will remain high

insights.claim: More frequent supply shocks and more hawkish central banks are the underlying causes behind persistently positive bond-stock correlations and elevated term premia.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Supply-shock news (for example energy disruptions) is likely to hit bonds and equities together, reducing diversification benefits.
